members.name: ArcDelegate
members.doc:
Bindings are owned by a shared block rather than by the delegate
itself so a Broadcast can keep walking after a handler destroys the
delegate (a button whose click closes the panel that owns it). A
copied delegate must not share that block — it would fire the
source's listeners — so copies deep-copy it.

members.name: Add
members.doc: The returned handle is what Remove takes

members.name: Add
members.signature: template<typename T> CDelegateHandle Add(T* obj, Ret (T::*method)(Args...))

members.name: Broadcast
members.doc:
Handlers may add or remove listeners, destroy the widget that owns
this delegate, or close the panel a LATER listener belongs to. The
walk therefore never touches `this` after the first call: it pins
the shared block, snapshots the handles, and before each call
re-resolves the handle against the live list — a listener removed
by an earlier handler is skipped rather than run against an object
that no longer exists. The functor is copied out before the call
because a handler that removes ITSELF would otherwise free the
storage it is executing from.

members.name: CacheDesiredSize
members.doc:
Recomputes the desired size only when something can have changed:
this widget or a descendant was invalidated, the layout scale moved,
or a global invalidation epoch fired. Also repairs the parent links
of every enumerable child so Invalidate() has a chain to walk.

members.name: CanCacheDesiredSize
members.doc:
Opt-in for the desired-size cache. A widget may only return true when
every input to its ComputeDesiredSize is either constant or routed
through Invalidate(): bound attributes, measure-reads-arrange feedback,
children generated during arrange, and children that are not reported
by GetChildAt all disqualify it. Default is false, so a widget nobody
audited keeps the previous always-recompute behaviour.

members.name: DesiredSizeDependsOnChildren
members.doc:
False when ComputeDesiredSize never reads a child size — a scroll
box, a list, a tree, a viewport: their measure is a constant and the
widgets under them are measured by their own arrange body instead.
The measure pass then stops here, where before it walked the whole
panel below to hash sizes that could not move this widget.

members.name: GetLayoutRevision
members.doc:
Bumped every time this widget's own inputs are invalidated. Anything
that memoizes a per-widget derived result (a text block's shaped
layout) keys on it instead of re-deriving the key from the inputs.

members.name: GetLayoutEpoch
members.doc:
The global invalidation epoch. A memo built from process-wide state
(the active style set, the font manager) is only valid while this
still matches, because InvalidateAllWidgets is what a style or font
swap announces itself with.

members.name: GetMeasureCount
members.doc:
How many ComputeDesiredSize calls CacheDesiredSize has let through.
The layout tests assert that a second pass over an unchanged tree
computes nothing at all; without a counter the only available
evidence would be a wall-clock delta, which proves nothing on a
loaded machine.

members.name: CanSkipArrange
members.doc:
Opt-in for the arrange skip. A widget may only return true when
ArrangeChildren is a pure function of the allotted geometry, its own
attributes and its children's cached desired sizes — and every input
that can move announces itself through Invalidate(). A body that
clamps a scroll offset, recycles rows, re-elides text against the
width it just handed out, or reads a clock disqualifies the widget:
skipping it would freeze the very thing the body exists to update.

The default answer is "yes" for a widget that reports no children,
because the base ArrangeChildren is empty and there is nothing to
freeze. Every widget that OVERRIDES ArrangeChildren therefore has to
state its own answer; one that stays silent reports children and is
refused by this default.

members.name: GetArrangeCount
SetArrangeSkipEnabled
members.doc:
Kill switch for the arrange skip, so a suspected stale-layout bug can
be confirmed or cleared in one process instead of across two builds.

members.name: OnPaint
members.signature: virtual int32_t OnPaint(const CArcPaintArgs& args, const CGeometry& allottedGeometry, CArcUIRenderer& renderer, int32_t layerId) const = 0

members.name: CanRetainPaint
members.doc:
Opt-in for the retained-paint cache. A widget may only return true
when its OnPaint output is a pure function of the arranged geometry,
its own attributes and its children — and every input that can move
announces itself through InvalidatePaint() (or Invalidate(), which
implies it). A bound attribute the body paints from, a running
animation, a blinking caret, a selection highlight, rows a view
recycles per frame, or a surface re-rendered every frame all
disqualify it: replaying would freeze exactly what the body exists
to update.

The default is false, so a widget nobody audited keeps painting.

members.name: InvalidatePaint
members.doc:
Drops this widget's retained paint and every ancestor slice that
contains it, without touching layout. This is the lighter sibling of
Invalidate(): hover, press, focus, a swatch colour — anything that
changes only what is drawn — belongs here, because invalidating the
layout for it would throw away a measure and an arrange that are
still correct.

The walk runs to the root rather than stopping at the first flagged
ancestor: only the OUTERMOST opted-in widget in a nesting run owns a
slice, so the widgets in between hold nothing to stop at and the
stale slice above them would survive.

members.name: InvalidateAllPaint
members.doc:
Drops every retained slice in the process without walking any tree.
The hammer for changes no widget can observe locally: a style set
swap, reloaded fonts, a font atlas rebuilt under already-baked glyph
UVs, a device pixel density change.

members.name: GetInvalidationSerial
members.doc:
Ticks on every invalidation of any kind anywhere — a layout or paint
walk, a slice dropped, a global drop. The window manager skips a
window's paint only while this has not moved since the window last
painted. Invalidations raised while a paint pass runs count apart:
a widget re-flagging itself mid-paint is judged by what it then
draws, and counting it here would let one window's paint keep every
other window from ever skipping.

members.name: SetInvalidationCensus
members.doc:
Counts, by widget type, the invalidations raised outside a paint pass
while on: the answer to "what keeps this window from skipping".

members.name: NoteLivePaint
members.doc:

members.doc:
Drop-target contract. While a drag operation is live the drag-drop
manager resolves the widget under the cursor on every move — the
widget holding mouse capture (the drag source) and its subtree are
skipped — and walks that path leaf to root offering the drag.

pass it up the path. A widget that declines must leave no state
behind, because it never receives OnDragLeave. The target then gets
OnDragOver on every move (return false to show the rejected cursor
without giving the target up) and exactly one OnDragLeave when the
cursor moves off it or the drag ends. OnDrop lands before that final
leave; returning true reports the drop as consumed.

their children through ArrangeChildWidget / PaintChildWidget — so

invalidation, because the transform lives in the arranged geometry
the hit test reads.

members.name: IsTextInput

members.name: ConsumesTab
members.doc:
True only for a widget that types Tab as a character (the multi-line
box). Every other text input lets Tab move focus, which is the only
way out of a single-line field from the keyboard.

members.name: GetFocusVisual
members.doc:

inputs answer None (their focused border says it); a row-like
widget answers InsetBorder.

members.name: PaintsOwnFocus
members.doc:
True for a widget whose own paint shows keyboard focus where the
framework's ring would be wrong (the ring round a slider's thumb,
a tree's or list's keyboard row): it answers None above and still
shows focus, which the keyboard audit has to know.

members.name: OwnsKeyboard
members.doc:
True while a self-drawn overlay (a command palette) holds the
keyboard the way a modal does: Tab is its own key there, so the
keyboard audit closes it with Escape before tabbing the window.

members.name: GetFocusRadius
members.doc:
The corner radius of the control's own outline. The focus ring is
drawn concentric with it (this plus the gap and stroke), so a pill
toggle gets a pill ring and a 2 px checkbox a near-square one; one
fixed radius made every ring a 4 px rounded box whatever it circled.

members.name: AllowsKeyBubbling
members.doc:
Whether a key this widget declined may be offered to its ancestors.
Overriding to false restores the pre-bubbling behaviour for this
widget and everything under it — the opt-out for a widget tree
(a game HUD arbitrating its own input, say) that must not have its
leftover keys reinterpreted by whatever it happens to be parented
to. The framework fallbacks still run; only the walk stops.

members.name: IsFocusable
members.doc:
Focusability predicate for directional (gamepad/keyboard)
navigation — the FNavigationConfig seam. Interactive widgets
override to true; navigation additionally requires the widget to
be visible and enabled.

members.name: OnActivate
members.doc:
A gamepad/keyboard accept aimed at this widget. Widgets translate
the activation internally (fire the click delegate, toggle, open)
instead of receiving a synthesized mouse click. Returns true when
the activation was consumed.

members.name: Invalidate
members.doc:
Marks this widget's desired size dirty, then walks up the parent chain
flagging ancestors. The walk stops at the first ancestor already
flagged — everything above it was flagged when it was.

members.name: NeedsSubtreeLayout
members.doc: True when this widget or anything below it needs a fresh measure.

members.name: InvalidateAllWidgets
members.doc:
Drops every cached desired size in the process, without walking any
tree. This is the hammer for changes no widget can observe locally:
active style set swapped, fonts reloaded, application scale changed.

members.name: SetFocusScopeId
members.doc:
The focus scope this widget roots, None on everything else. The
command system walks from the focused widget to the root, collects
the scopes named along the way and offers a chord to them innermost
first, before the pushed lists and the global keymap. That is what
makes a shortcut follow the panel the user is in; the editor used to
scope by pointer hover, which retargeted the chord the moment the
mouse drifted off the panel mid-edit. Focus itself is unchanged —
OnFocusReceived/OnFocusLost and CReply::SetUserFocus still own it,
and a scope is only read off the path they produce.

types.name: AWidget::FArrangeScope
types.doc:
Guard every opted-in ArrangeChildren body opens with. It answers
whether the arrange can be skipped, and on destruction — so early
returns are covered — records the geometry this pass ran with and
re-folds the subtree's skippability.
Only the two functions are exported, not the class: dllexporting a
type with a reference member and a by-value CGeometry buys nothing
and costs a C4251 per translation unit that includes this header.

types.name: AWidget::FRetainedPaintCensus
types.doc:
Where retention stands across a tree, per widget type: how many
opted in, how many have given up, how many proved their subtree and
how many hold a slice a clean frame could replay. Read by the
bench, because a low replay count says only that something is
wrong and this says where.

types.name: AWidget::FPaintScope
types.doc:
Guard an opted-in container's OnPaint opens with. It answers whether
the subtree can be replayed and, on destruction — so early returns
are covered — closes the recording and re-folds the subtree.

A leaf needs no scope: its parent's slice already contains it, and
the fold accepts a childless widget on CanRetainPaint() alone. Only
a widget that paints children has to open one, because a container
that opted in without folding would veto every ancestor above it.
Only the functions are exported, not the class: dllexporting a type
with reference members and a by-value CGeometry buys nothing and
costs a C4251 per translation unit that includes this header.

members.name: ArrangeStack
members.signature: void ArrangeStack(const std::vector<float>& cardHeights, float windowHeight, const FToastArea& area, float deltaTime, bool snap)

so a new card never moves the ones already up. cardHeights is one

line at the bottom: the newest card is always shown. Each card's
StackOffset eases toward its slot over deltaTime; snap places
every card at once (a different window took the stack).

members.name: RenderOwnedWindows
members.doc:
Renders and presents only the Arc-owned swapchain windows, skipping
wrapped/external ones, all on the calling thread. Host engines call

manager — PaintMainWindow already did.

members.name: ProduceOwnedWindows
members.doc:
RenderOwnedWindows in three parts for a host that records on its
own rendering thread. Produce runs on the game thread (layout,
paint, batch snapshot) and pins each window's batch; Record opens
each window's frame, records the pinned batch and closes it; Present
hands each recorded window to its swapchain's deferred present.
Record and Present touch no widget and no platform window, so they
may run on another thread while the game thread produces the next
frame. The windows stay alive until the record fence (below) ran.

members.name: SetRecordFence
members.doc:

before any window's GPU side is torn down; a host recording owned
windows on another thread must install it.

members.name: HasOwnedWindowsToRender
members.doc:
True when RenderOwnedWindows would record at least one window. A
host that must fence its render thread before that recording asks
first, so a frame with no floating panel or popup keeps its overlap.

members.name: DismissTooltip
members.doc:

pointer moves again. Every mouse press routes through here, as does
every popup that opens and every loss of window focus.

members.name: SetOSPopupsEnabled

topmost) so they can overhang the owning window like every native
app. On by default; when off — or when popup creation fails — the
legacy in-window overlay painting takes over.

members.name: SetPopupsInWindowWhenTheyFit

A menu or tooltip that fits inside its owning window paints there,
as Slate does, and only one that must overhang the window gets an
OS window of its own. Each OS popup costs a swapchain, a command
buffer and a renderer, and every one of those once drained the GPU
on the game thread: the owner's 1-19 s stalls sat next to popup
creation and resizes. On by default.

Inject a platform event directly (for host engines that own the SDL event loop).
Call this instead of ProcessEvents() when the host polls SDL events itself.

types.name: CArcTouchGestureFilter
types.doc:
M4.2 touch feel. Touch pointer events (IsTouch, translated by the SDL
backend from the primary finger) run through a deferred-press state
machine before they reach widget routing:

- finger down forwards NOTHING until the gesture resolves — a
finger wobbles 5-10 px even when the user means a plain tap, and
forwarding raw motion turns every tap into an accidental drag
against the widgets' 4-5 px mouse thresholds;
- lift inside the slop radius = tap: the held-back press and the
release are forwarded back-to-back at the press point;
- motion beyond the slop = drag: the held-back press is forwarded
at the press point, then the motions flow through live;
- holding inside the slop past the delay = long-press: a
right-button click (down+up) is synthesized — the touch idiom for
"context menu" — and the eventual lift is swallowed.

Coordinates are Arc logical units, which are already DPI-normalized,
so the slop is a plain constant. Mouse events pass through untouched.

types.name: EArcTextDirection
types.doc:
A paragraph's base direction. Auto is UAX #9's P2/P3: the first strong

types.name: CArcBidi
types.doc:
The Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm (UAX #9) over one paragraph of
codepoints: explicit embeddings, overrides and isolates (X1-X10), weak and
neutral resolution including bracket pairs (W1-W7, N0-N2), implicit
levels (I1-I2), the paragraph half of L1, and line reordering (L2).
HarfBuzz shapes a run in a direction it is given; this is what decides
the direction and the run boundaries, which Arc used to hard-wire to LTR.

Written in-tree rather than vendored: the property data is a compact range
table of the classes that matter for layout (every RTL script block, the
numerals, the separators and terminators, the explicit formatting
characters, the marks of the scripts that sit beside RTL text), with
unlisted codepoints taking their block's default. ValidateTables pins that
the tables stay sorted, which the binary search depends on.

Shapes at the device pixel size fontSize maps to under rasterScale
and converts the result back to logical units, so every advance and
offset is a whole number of device pixels. Hinted advances taken at

types.name: ARetainerBox
types.doc:
A retainer: it renders its child subtree into an offscreen layer and
composites that image once, so the group opacity applies to the subtree
as a whole rather than to each child in turn. With a phase count above
one the image persists between frames: the subtree is painted only on
the frames its phase owns, and every other frame redraws the kept image
without walking the subtree. Without layer support (no device, a
transformed ancestor) it falls back to per-child opacity and paints
every frame.
